George B. Lennox is now a travelling man - after trying many ventures in up-State cities and towns, Mr. Lennox has finally struck the job he claims is his - travelling. For more than a month, Mr. Lennox and his family have been living in his unique hotel on the Leister estate on the upper end of Manhattan. Mr. Lennox a handy man with carpenters tools has made his own hotel, for his wife and daughter and with this novel residence will sooner or later begin his drive to the coast. In this way he plans to greatly reduce his cost of living and at the same time get all the enjoyment possible out of life. Will some please tell the people of Seabright, N.J., what to do when a resident paints gross libels on his spite fence and departs the premises with a shot gun, defying anyone to touch the fence. James M. Allgor is the originator of this puzzling condition of affairs. He defended his arithmetic neighbors by turning his cottage into an ice crew parlor. When they said nasty things about him he built a six foot fence around the property and said very nasty things about them, or rather caused his spite fence to convey the news to all and sundry that some of the residents were robbers, others smugglers, some ought to be in jail and others by rights though be in the place that is only expressed with one letter and a dash. Libel suits were brought against Allgor because of his highly personal spite fence and the court decided against him. Now he defies the courts, his neighbors and the entire community to make him take his fence down or obliterate one letter of the sizzling statements concerning his neighbors, the mayor, the police and others. With a shot gun over his shoulder he patrols the property and says he means business. One of these days, when the time comes for the court's edict to be enforced there will probably be some interesting news from this exclusive summer resort.

LONDON'S DREAM CITY
Permanent Pleasure Resort To Be Opened Next Spring.
ENGLISH CONEY ISLAND.
London is to have a "Dream City"—a permanent amusement park wherein all may reveal in delights which even Coney Island—beloved of the New Yorker—will have hard work to surpass.

The site of this entertainment colony is in Bat- tsersea. Fifteen acres of ground, formerly taken up by the Metropolitan Water Board's filter-beds and reservoirs, have been secured on a twenty-one years' lease by a British-American enterprise.
Next May is to witness the opening of this English Coney Island, which is but three-quarters of a mile from Victoria Station, and easily accessible from all parts.

A landmark will be a tower 300ft. high, to be illuminated by over 10,000 electric lamps. Fronting the river will be a café-restaurant 200ft. long with a terrace 40ft. wide. Here visitors will be able to partake of tea to the accompaniment of music played by regimental bands.

Open-air attractions will, of course, be endless. Roof gardens, ornamental grounds and lakes, beautiful walks and terraces, an exhibition palace and theatre, will be amongst the principal features of this city of amusement.
GLOOM-DISPELLING BRILLIANCE.

Beauty and brightness, mirth and music everywhere, is the aim of the city's founders, and a blaze of 100,000 electric lamps will dispel any gloom that our variable climate may try to foist upon us. But it is in the matter of amusement that Dream City means to excel.

"We are engaging the most famous 'turns' it is possible to obtain," Mr. B. Frankel, who directs this important part of the administration, told the Daily Mirror yesterday. "All the greatest novelties will find their way to Dream City."

"A large exhibition building, given up to different exhibits from time to time, is to be erected, and there will be a dancing hall. One of the most attractive features will be the submarines, in which visitors will be able to descend with perfect safety into the lakes."
Dream City will be approachable by water as well as land, for a pier is to be erected, so that river steamers may disembark their passengers.
POPULAR WINTER RESORT

Outside the main building one half of the grounds remaining will be laid out so as to represent miniature gardens of the different countries of the world. The other half will be monopolised by amusement enterprises.
Londoners have frequently deplored the fact that the capital has not enough popular resorts calculated to enliven the dread monotony of the winter months.

But Dream City only has to "catch on," and then, instead of closing in October, like the majority of exhibitions, the promoters of this latest enterprise may be encouraged to make it an "all-the-year-round" attraction.

A charge of sixpence-half-price for children—for admittance is to be instituted, so that Dream City may have full opportunity of becoming a popular resort in every sense of the word.

ROUGH BOYS

Dear Editor,-I am greatly interested in the pastime which those who take part in it call "sport," namely, stag-hunting.

In my opinion, it is just as great a crime as the bull-fighting of Spain. To goad and terrify a poor, harmless beast is most revolting, and the sooner an Act of Parliament is brought into force, abolishing such practices, the better. Surely Englishmen can be sportsmen without being cruel?
Hossey PHILIP STANLEY.

HISTORY LESSONS

Dear Editor.—One of the things that is decidedly wrong in school teaching is that every child is forced to learn history dates. It makes the child hate the history lessons, when it would probably otherwise love them. Why should we be forced to know the date of every coronation? Surely it is enough to know the reign and century in which an event happened, instead of cramming a child's head with dates? Of course, it is very nice to know them, but I think it is quite unnecessary, unless the teacher's aim is to turn her pupils into walking encyclopedias.

FLAT.

The increase of flat life has made a great difference in the amount of domestic work to be done, but it has not been met by any change in the attitude of that most conservative of beings, the domestic servants.

A large number of fairly well-to-do middle-class people have taken to flats as a step in the direction of the simple life. They have reduced the amount of work to be done to the capacities of one competent servant, but that servant is not forthcoming.

Hitherto the general servant has typically been $n$ overworked person, ill-paid, and doing her work correspondingly badly. There is no reason why the new general servant should not be as well trained for her job as the specialist cook or parlourmaid, or why she should receive less wages.

Cannot those enterprising ladies who aim at the well-being of servants and their employers give their mind to the evolution of the much-needed new type of servant and to the removal of the stigma which has hitherto attached to the name "general servant"?
